chunks: Indeed, for Allah there are two Intentions and two Desires — an Absolute Intention and a Determined Intention. He forbids while He desires, and He commands while He does not desire.

Or did you not see that He forbade Adam and his wife from eating from the tree, and yet He desired that — and had He not desired that they eat, their desire would not have prevailed over the Desire of Allah the Exalted.
And He commanded Ibrahim to slaughter Ishaq, and He did not desire that he slaughter him — and had He so desired, the desire of Ibrahim would not have prevailed over the Desire of Allah the Exalted.

key_terms.إِرَادَةَ حَتْمٍ: Absolute Intention — the divine will that is absolutely decreed to occur; corresponds to God's creative/existential will
key_terms.إِرَادَةَ عَزْمٍ: Determined Intention — the divine will expressed as a command or prohibition; corresponds to God's legislative will
key_terms.غَلَبَتْ: prevailed/overcame — used to demonstrate the impossibility of any creature's will overriding God's absolute will
key_terms.مَشِيئَة: Mashi'a — Divine Desire or Will; here distinguished from Irada to capture two layers of divine volition

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between God's legislative will and His creative will in Shia theology?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam Abu al-Hasan (likely al-Ridha, AS) presents a sophisticated theological framework distinguishing between two divine modes of will: an 'Absolute Intention' (iradat hatm) — what God ultimately decrees to occur — and a 'Determined Intention' (iradat 'azm) — what God commands as a normative duty. The examples of Adam and the forbidden tree, and Ibrahim's command to sacrifice Ishaq, illustrate how God may forbid something while internally desiring that it happens (to fulfill a higher purpose), or command something while not desiring it to fully execute (to test obedience). This distinction resolves the apparent contradiction between God's legislative will (what He commands/forbids) and His creative/existential will (what He decrees to occur), a central debate in Islamic theology addressing human free will and divine sovereignty.
